title: A/B Testing Foundations: From Hypothesis to Decision
description: Master the core mechanics of A/B testing including hypothesis design, statistical significance, confidence intervals, and common experiment pitfalls.

interactions.prompt: What is the null hypothesis in Spotify's test?

options.text: The new layout will increase engagement significantly
There is no difference in engagement between the two layouts
The old layout is better than the new one
Users prefer whichever layout they see first

interactions.teachingPreamble: Every A/B test starts with a null hypothesis  -  the assumption that there's no difference between your control and variant. For example, Spotify might test a new playlist layout by assuming it won't change user engagement. The goal of the experiment is to gather enough evidence to reject this null hypothesis.

interactions.prompt: Airbnb runs a booking flow test: Control converts at 3.2% (n=50,000), Variant at 3.4% (n=50,000). The p-value is 0.12. What's the key takeaway?

options.text: The variant is clearly better  -  ship it immediately
The result is not statistically significant; we can't confirm a real difference
The sample size was too small to detect anything
A 0.2% lift is never worth pursuing

interactions.prompt: If Netflix uses a 95% confidence interval of [+1.2%, +3.8%] for a new recommendation algorithm's lift, what does this mean?

options.text: There's a 95% chance the true lift is between 1.2% and 3.8%
Exactly 95% of users experienced a lift in that range
The test will be significant 95% of the time it's repeated
The algorithm works for 95% of users

interactions.teachingPreamble: A confidence interval gives you a range of plausible values for the true effect of your change. When Netflix tests a new recommendation algorithm and gets a 95% CI of [+1.2%, +3.8%], it means they're 95% confident the real impact falls within that range. If the interval doesn't cross zero, the result is statistically significant.

interactions.prompt: In A/B testing, a ____ error means concluding a variant wins when it actually doesn't  -  also called a false positive.

options.text: Type I
Type II
Sampling
Standard

interactions.prompt: Your e-commerce team's A/B test on a new checkout flow shows a +5% conversion lift after 3 days, with p=0.04. But the pre-registered test duration was 14 days. Do you ship early or wait?

options.text: Ship now  -  p<0.05 proves the variant wins
Wait the full 14 days to avoid peeking bias
Ship to 50% of traffic as a compromise
Restart the test with a larger sample size

interactions.prompt: Why is this a problem for DoorDash's experiment?

options.text: It makes the test run too long
Heavy users skew results, masking the experience of typical customers
It reduces the total sample size available
It always inflates conversion rates in the control group

interactions.teachingPreamble: Sample Ratio Mismatch (SRM) and selection bias are silent killers of experiments. Imagine DoorDash tests a new delivery ETA display, but power users who order 5x per week generate disproportionate data compared to occasional users. This creates a biased sample where conclusions are driven by a non-representative subset of your audience.

interactions.prompt: You're designing an A/B test for Slack's new onboarding flow. Rank these steps in the correct order from first to last.

options.text: Analyze results and check for statistical significance
Define your hypothesis and choose a primary metric
Calculate required sample size and set test duration
Randomize users into control and variant groups

interactions.prompt: Halfway through your 14-day test, engineering deploys a site-wide performance upgrade that cuts page load time by 40% for all users. What should you do?

options.text: Continue the test  -  both groups are equally affected
Stop and restart the test to isolate your variable cleanly
Analyze only the data collected before the deployment
Extend the test duration by another 14 days

interactions.priorContext: You had a well-designed 14-day A/B test running on a checkout flow redesign. Now a major external change  -  a 40% site-wide speed improvement  -  has been introduced mid-experiment, potentially changing baseline user behavior and invalidating the controlled conditions you established.
